title: Crash in [@ mozilla::net::nsHttpChannel::ContinueProcessResponse1] and ContinueProcessResponse3 on null mAuthProvider
body: I found a new release crash signature through the crash spike detector: EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION_READ in mozilla::net::nsHttpChannel::ContinueProcessResponse1. A similar ContinueProcessResponse3 signature may be the same issue. Looking at about half a dozen reports, the crash is on `rv = mAuthProvider->CheckForSuperfluousAuth();`, so I suspect `mAuthProvider` may be null.

symptoms_visible: I am seeing release crash reports with EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION_READ in ContinueProcessResponse1, with the failing line calling CheckForSuperfluousAuth through mAuthProvider.
I am also seeing a similar ContinueProcessResponse3 crash signature.
N0.label: N0 release null-access crash reported

symptoms_visible: On my affected enterprise setup, including the invalid autoadmin.global_config_url in mozilla.cfg and restarting twice makes Firefox download config.pac through the forced system proxy configuration and then crash.
N1.label: N1 proxy and enterprise autoconfig reproduction established

symptoms_visible: Firefox still crashes with network.auth.use_redirect_for_retries set to false; when I tried setting it to true, it was back to false after the crash report.
N2.label: N2 redirect-for-retries preference probed

symptoms_visible: Firefox still crashes in the reproducible proxy and autoconfig setup while HTTP file logging is enabled.
N3.label: N3 HTTP crash log collected

N_terminal.label: terminal crash stopped after null-guard update

question_patterns: Can anyone reproduce this crash reliably, and what proxy or enterprise configuration is active?
What changes between a working startup and a crashing startup?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I can reproduce it with Firefox set to use the system proxy configuration, which is also forced by our Autoconfig file. The difference is including `lockPref("autoadmin.global_config_url", "http://internal-server/invalid-url/firefox.js");` in mozilla.cfg. After I include it and restart Firefox twice, Firefox downloads a 51 KB config.pac from the Windows automatic configuration script setting and then crashes.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The enterprise configuration produces a different crash signature, and its report does not contain ContinueProcessResponse1, ContinueProcessResponse3, or the CheckForSuperfluousAuth line.
The same crash occurs with a different unreachable internal URL in the autoadmin.global_config_url setting.

question_patterns: Do the other crash reports mention any common network, proxy, or authentication setup?
Is there a pattern in the comments attached to the crash reports?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I found one crash comment describing saved proxy authentication with the option not to prompt again, followed by a crash on the next startup. Another comment says version 128 crashes when a proxy is configured.

edges.comment: Real thread c4-c7: participant1 supplied the reproducible enterprise Autoconfig/system-proxy setup and the reporter supplied matching proxy-authentication comments from other crash reports. These affected users are folded into one simulated user side; participant1's machines produced the same crash family as the opening report.

question_patterns: Can you test both values of network.auth.use_redirect_for_retries and report what happens?
Please check the current value of network.auth.use_redirect_for_retries, toggle it for a test, and tell me whether Firefox still crashes.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I already had that option set to false and created another crash report with it false. I also tried setting it to true, but after reporting the crash I noticed it was set to false again. The Autoconfig URL line remains the only difference between the working and crashing setups.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Setting the preference to false prevents the crash consistently across restarts, while setting it to true immediately brings the crash back.
The preference was false on both affected PCs, and both still produced the same crash.

edges.comment: Real thread c8-c10: participant2 proposed the preference probe and participant1 supplied raw crash outcomes from a second PC. This is a handler-initiated configuration measurement, not a solution edge; the user does not claim which code path the result implicates.

question_patterns: Could you reproduce the crash with HTTP logging to a file enabled and send the resulting log?
Please capture an HTTP log from an affected startup, using logging to a file because Firefox crashes.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Log sent. It is from the first PC, whose crash report was d8da664a-8543-4bb6-87c5-482a50240722; the two preference-test crash reports were from the second PC.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: I used a different filename for the HTTP log, but it came from the same first PC and crashing startup.

edges.comment: Real thread c11-c12: participant3 requested file-based HTTP logging and participant1 sent the log privately, distinguishing the first reproduction PC from the second PC used for the preference probe. No log interpretation was published, so none is placed in the user's answer.

solution.intent: Prevent the release crash by guarding mAuthProvider before it is dereferenced in the affected response-continuation paths and aborting response processing safely when it is null, while explicitly treating this as a crash-stop workaround because the reason the provider becomes null is still unknown.
solution.concrete_example: Add null checks before the vulnerable mAuthProvider uses in ContinueProcessResponse1 and ContinueProcessResponse3 and return safely if the provider is absent. This stops the null dereference but does not yet explain why mAuthProvider became null. Once the change is available, ask the affected user to retest in today's build and report whether it still crashes.
solution.inference_hint: The crash reports expose the access-violation line and the user supplies proxy/autoconfig reproduction, preference-test output, and an HTTP log. Concluding that the immediate failure is a null mAuthProvider dereference is engineer-side confirmation. The thread explicitly states later that the null checks only stop the crash and that the reason mAuthProvider becomes null was not determined.

edges.comment: Real thread c13-c28: participant3 authored null checks for mAuthProvider; maintainers described the behavior as aborting when the provider is null. Participant3 later clarified that this was only a workaround and that the underlying null state remained unexplained. After installing the build containing the landed change, participant1 reported that Firefox no longer crashed and sent fresh logs. Uplift approvals and release coordination are intentionally not scored.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted immediate cause: ContinueProcessResponse1 and ContinueProcessResponse3 can dereference a null mAuthProvider; the underlying reason it becomes null remains unknown.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the crash line and collected affected-user evidence, including the reproducible proxy/enterprise-Autoconfig setup, preference probe, and HTTP-log collection; it must not invent unpublished findings from the privately sent log.

The technical remedy must add null guards around the affected mAuthProvider uses and abort safely when it is absent, while describing this accurately as a crash-stop workaround rather than a complete causal fix.
Must not recommend network.auth.use_redirect_for_retries=false as the resolution: the affected setup already had it false and still crashed.
Must ask an affected user to verify a build containing the fix and must not declare resolution until the user reports that the crash no longer occurs.

persona_hint.experience_level: A merged affected-user side consisting of a technically experienced crash triager who reads stacks and source code plus an enterprise Firefox user who can edit mozilla.cfg, inspect proxy preferences, reproduce across two PCs, submit crash reports, and capture HTTP logs.
persona_hint.communication_style: Concise, evidence-driven, and cooperative. Supplies exact crash IDs, configuration lines, preference values, and machine distinctions; clearly labels uncertainty and does not infer conclusions from diagnostic output.
